description:
At the September 2, 2025, Historic Preservation Board (HPB) meeting, the Board held an in-depth discussion on preservation priorities, potential ordinance updates, and expanded local recognition of historic structures. Chairman Kiesel emphasized the importance of the City of Titusville supporting historic preservation initiatives. Chairman Kiesel recommended updating or amending the City’s ordinance to align with Senate Bill 582, which strengthens local historic preservation authority. Chairman Kiesel asked whether the HPB could play a larger role in reviewing demolitions of historic structures. Mr. Parrish responded that this would require a change to the ordinance. Chairman Kiesel requested further discussion on this issue at future meetings.
The enclosed memo from the City's Historic Preservation Officer (HPO), Pat Tyjeski, provides an overview of the City's historic property demolition provisions, a peer review analysis, and suggestions for updating Titusville's historic preservation regulations to improve the monitoring and management of building demolitions within the City.
On December 1, 2025, the Board recommended the report from Historic Preservation Officer Pat Tyjeski with her stated recommendations and flow-chart be forwarded to City Council for consideration.
title: Historic Preservation Ordinance

description:
At the August 12, 2025 Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) meeting, the Broad Street Streetscape was unanimously approved by the CRA Board. The Broad Street project is envisioned as a signature downtown “festival street” that supports community events, enhances walkability, and strengthens economic activity within the Downtown Titusville CRA District. The City maintains continuing service agreements with two engineering firms to support public works projects. These firms possess specialized technical expertise and adequate resources and are engaged on a rotating, as-needed basis to provide engineering services. In accordance with the existing contract for professional consulting services, the firm of AECOM Technical Services, Inc.("Consultant") has been requested to provide a proposal for scope of services outlining the professional design services required to advance the project from data collection and conceptual design through final construction documents.
Project Limits
The Broad Street project area is located within downtown Titusville and generally extends from Lemon Avenue South on the west to the parking area near Veterans Memorial Park on the east, encompassing approximately 1,950 linear feet within a 100-foot right-of-way. The corridor includes multiple intersections, including two FDOT-owned U.S. 1 crossings, which will require coordination with FDOT standards and requirements.
Overall Scope and Approach
AECOM’s scope is structured to deliver a comprehensive, phased design process. The work includes project administration, site data collection, conceptual design, stakeholder engagement, and preparation of 30%, 60%, and final signed and sealed construction documents. Permitting and construction administration services are excluded and would require a separate authorization.
Project Administration
AECOM will manage the consultant team, coordinate with City and CRA staff, conduct a formal kickoff meeting, and facilitate up to sixteen progress meetings throughout the design process. Written summaries and meeting documentation will be provided to ensure transparency and coordination.
Site Data Collection and Analysis
The consultant team will complete detailed topographic, boundary, tree, and subsurface utility surveys, along with a geotechnical investigation. This work will ensure a site base plan and a strengths-weaknesses-opportunities-threats (SWOT) analysis to guide design decisions and identify constraints early in the process.
Concept Design and Visioning
AECOM will prepare up to two conceptual design alternatives, supported by 3-D visualizations and precedent imagery. Following City selection of a preferred alternative, a Final Concept Plan Package will be prepared to illustrate the overall vision for Broad Street, including paving treatments, landscaping, and site furnishings
Stakeholder and CRA Engagement
The scope includes a dedicated stakeholder meeting and a separate CRA input meeting to gather feedback on the concept design. A summary of input received will be prepared and presented to City and CRA staff to inform refinement of the design.
Design Development (30%, 60%, and Final Plans)
AECOM will advance the approved concept into detailed construction documents in three phases. Each phase includes updated plans, specifications, and cost estimates, allowing the City and CRA to evaluate scope, design, and budget as the project progresses. Elements addressed include grading and drainage, hardscape, landscaping, irrigation, lighting, utilities coordination, and evaluation of EV charging capabilities.
Schedule and Budget
The anticipated design schedule totals approximately 38 weeks, excluding City review periods. The total lump-sum cost for the base scope of services is $440,825, with fees allocated by task and milestone. An optional wayfinding and signage design task is available for $25,130 if authorized by the City and CRA. There is $280,515 in the Broad Street Parking Account. Staff is recommending a budget adjustment of $65,847 from the Space View Pier and $94,463 from the CRA Restricted Fun Balance Account.
It is recommended that City Council approve the Continuing Consultant Contract CO23Q006 Task Order 9 with AECOM Technologies Inc. in the amount of $440,825 to provide Consulting and Design Services for the Broad Street Streetscape project and authorize the City Manager to execute the task order and approve the associated budget amendment.
title: Continuing Contract CO23Q006 Task Order 9 with AECOM Inc. for Broad Street Design

description:
On August 8, 2023, Council approved the City’s use of Brevard County Contract #10047 (RFP #7-22-07), effective through March 2026, with DEX Imaging for the lease and maintenance of multifunction office equipment. Through this piggyback agreement, DEX Imaging provided the City with new equipment, along with maintenance, toner, staples, and paper, at a lower lease rate than the City was previously paying.
The City’s current annual lease cost is $20,970.53, with maintenance fees of $0.03983 per color click and $0.01159 per black-and-white click. Based on estimated annual usage of 286,701 color clicks and 717,110 black-and-white clicks, total maintenance annual costs are estimated at $19,730.62.
As the existing contract approaches its expiration in March 2026, DEX Imaging has provided the City with a written offer to extend the lease for an additional five (5) years at the same lease rate currently in effect for the City’s copiers. Extending the agreement would allow the City to secure fixed pricing established under the 2023 contract and avoid exposure to higher current market rates, thereby stabilizing future expenditures. The annual lease and maintenance fees would remain fixed for the entire term of the extension.
Because the City received new multifunction copier equipment in 2023, the equipment is expected to have a minimum of five years of remaining service life, making it suitable for the proposed extension period. Additionally, extending the current lease would minimize operational disruptions to City departments by retaining existing equipment and avoiding the need for replacement or transition to a new vendor.
Brevard County’s copier equipment is nearing the end of its service life and will require the County to solicit a new contract subject to current market pricing. Both the County and City staff have reviewed alternative national purchasing cooperative contracts and have not identified any options that provide lower lease rates or more favorable terms than those currently available through DEX Imaging.
There is no increase in the annual lease rate as a result of the proposed extension. Costs will remain consistent with the current budgeted amounts, subject to actual usage for maintenance charges.
It is recommended that City Council approve extension of a 5-year lease and maintenance of the City’s current multi-functional copiers at an estimated $40,700 annually and authorize the City Manager to execute all required agreement documents and City staff to issue the necessary purchase orders.
title: Lease of Multi-Functional Copiers

description:
The proposed Ordinance amends the City of Titusville Police Officers' and Firefighters' Pension Plan. The special incentives for Firefighters that are specified in the Pension Plan are also referred to in the Firefighters Collective Bargaining Agreement. As a practical matter, these incentives are referred to in the most recent Collective Bargaining Agreement dated November 24, 2024 and are subject to change each year through the bargaining process. So the proposed Ordinance provides for a change in the types of incentive pay pursuant to the Collective Bargaining Agreement.
Insofar as combining the two amendments, the Pension Board is recommending a clarification amendment to the Plan recommended by its Actuary to the manner in which earnings are calculated for DROP accounts. The Board is amending its methodology in valuing DROP II accounts to provide for quarterly, instead of yearly, interest and earnings. A member who separates from participation in their DROP II and separates from their employment with the City will now receive earnings from their DROP II account determined as of the most recent quarterly net investment return prior to the member's separation.

description: On October 14, 2025, Mr. Jesse Wright requested the City Council consider amending the list of permitted uses in the Urban Village (UV) zoning district to include schools. Enclosed for Council's information is a list of Conditional Use Permit requests to establish a new school or to modify existing schools between the years 2017 and 2025. Section 28-255 of the City's Land Development Regulations defines schools (public or private) as any building or group of buildings or part thereof which is designed, constructed or used for educational or instruction of any branch of knowledge. The same Section further lists the zoning districts where schools are permitted, permitted with limitations, and permitted with a conditional use permit. A conditional use permit is required in all residential and commercial zoning districts. It is therefore recommended that a school in the UV zoning district also require a conditional use permit. Enclosed for Council's review is a draft ordinance.

description:
TPD is responsible for communicating timely, accurate, and appropriate public-safety information during major criminal investigations, critical incidents, emergency events, officer-involved incidents, threats to public safety, and other complex or high-profile law-enforcement matters. These incidents frequently require specialized communication strategies that extend beyond the Department’s routine public-information and community-relations functions. Inaccurate, delayed, or uncoordinated messaging may interfere with investigative objectives, contribute to the spread of misinformation, affect public safety, and diminish community confidence in law-enforcement operations.
The purpose of this request is for City Council authorization to enter into a professional‑services agreement with Cole Pro Media to support the Police Department’s strategic communications, transparency efforts, and critical‑incident response needs. Cole Pro Media provides a unique, highly specialized service tailored specifically to law‑enforcement agencies navigating complex operational, reputational, and transparency obligations.
Key factors supporting the selection of Cole Pro Media include:Exclusive specialization in law‑enforcement strategic communications, transparency advisory services, community‑trust messaging, and critical‑incident reporting.
Proven capability in producing Critical Incident Videos—an increasingly essential tool for modern public‑safety agencies.
Leadership experience that includes former White House correspondence and professional news reporting, along with active involvement in the Florida Police Chiefs Association (FPCA).
A physical presence in Fort Lauderdale, which provides regional familiarity and enhanced responsiveness to Florida agencies.
Vendor Evaluation and Comparative Analysis
To ensure due diligence, the Department evaluated other reputable strategic‑communications vendors. While each firm offers value, they do not provide the specialized, law‑enforcement‑specific capabilities required for the City’s needs.
Cole Pro Media (Recommended Vendor)Specializes in public‑safety and law‑enforcement communications, including crisis communications, transparency advisory, rapid‑response messaging, media strategy, and executive communications coaching.
Offers Critical Incident Videos, a highly relevant and distinguishing capability.
Founder’s experience includes work as a White House correspondent and broadcast journalist, with significant engagement in FPCA activities.
Strong alignment with high‑profile, sensitive public‑safety incidents such as use‑of‑force cases, officer‑involved shootings, and releases of controversial video content.
Based in Fort Lauderdale, enabling immediate responsiveness and familiarity with Florida public‑safety agencies.
Julie Parker Communications (Not Selected)Provides broad crisis‑communications and media‑relations services, including spokesperson coaching, media strategy, internal communications, and long‑term retainer support.
Experienced in handling major incidents, natural disasters, civil unrest, and reputational crises.
Best suited for agencies seeking an embedded, long‑term communications strategist rather than a highly specialized, incident‑focused public‑safety partner.
Limitation: The firm is located out of state, reducing operational proximity and real‑time responsiveness for Florida‑based agencies.
Bold Thinkers Group (Not Selected)Offers crisis‑communications services with a strong FEMA/emergency‑management orientation, including PIO training, media relations, post‑crisis recovery, and technical services such as web and video production.
Well‑suited for agencies seeking alignment with FEMA doctrine, PIO training, or broad communications infrastructure support.
Limitation: Less specialized in law‑enforcement transparency and critical‑incident reporting; primary focus appears oriented toward emergency management rather than police-specific communications.
The proposed services will provide the Department with additional professional expertise that is not otherwise available. The agreement is intended to supplement, not replace, the Department’s existing communications responsibilities and approved operating budget.
It is recommended that the City Council approve the Police Department’s request to single‑source Cole Pro Media as the City’s strategic law enforcement communications partner for public‑safety and critical‑incident communications and approve the budget amendment to utilize restricted forfeiture funds in the amount of $24,000.00 for the one year term.
title: Cole Pro Media Professional Services Agreement

description:
The TPD continues to evaluate proactive strategies to address firearm-related crime and reduce the availability of unwanted firearms within the community. Recent incidents involving firearms, including incidents involving youth, reinforce the importance of developing additional crime-prevention strategies designed to reduce opportunities for firearms to be unlawfully possessed, stolen, transferred, or used in criminal activity.
As part of this effort, the TPD proposes conducting several firearm buyback events throughout the FY27. These events will provide community members with an opportunity to voluntarily surrender unwanted firearms to law enforcement as part of a structured crime-prevention initiative.
While firearm buyback programs represent only one component of a comprehensive violence-reduction strategy, they provide law enforcement with an additional opportunity to remove unwanted firearms from circulation, reduce the potential for unsecured firearms to be stolen or accessed by youth, encourage responsible firearm disposition, and engage directly with neighborhoods experiencing firearm-related violence.
The Department intends to strategically conduct these events within or near areas impacted by firearm-related incidents and utilize the initiative in conjunction with existing enforcement, investigative, youth-outreach, community-engagement, and crime-prevention efforts. The proposed firearm buyback initiative represents a supplemental crime-prevention and safe-neighborhood program and is not part of the Department's normal operating budget. The requested funds will be dedicated specifically to supporting the program and will not replace existing General Fund expenditures.
title: Firearm Buyback and Crime Prevention Program

The property also satisfies Condition 5 because providing service will not overload the existing water system. The City has sufficient capacity to serve the proposed single-family residence, which is allocated 300 gallons per day pursuant to the City of Titusville Concurrency Management Manual.

description:
The applicant is requesting a rezoning (REZ) of approximately 7.5 acres located at 1915 N Singleton Avenue, generally east of N Singleton Avenue, between Parrish Road to the north and Kirby Drive to the south (Brevard County Parcel ID No. 21-35-20-00-535). The request is to change the zoning from Single-Family Medium Density (R-1B) to General Use (GU).
The applicant intends to use the property for agricultural purposes (farming). Agricultural uses are not permitted in the current R-1B zoning district but are permitted with limitations in the requested GU zoning district, as indicated by an “L” in the zoning Use Table.
The subject property was annexed into the City in 2004 through Ordinance No. 31-2004. At that time, the property was part of a larger 15-acre parcel that included the 7.5-acre parcel immediately to the north (Brevard County Parcel ID No. 21-35-20-00-534). At the same meeting, City Council adopted Ordinance No. 35-2004, which designated the property’s future land use as Low Density Residential.
Ordinance No. 31-2004 established the current R-1B zoning and, in Section 4, limited the entire 15-acre parcel to a maximum of 50 residential units. This limitation is more restrictive than the R-1B zoning district’s maximum density of 5.8 dwelling units per acre, which would otherwise allow up to 87 units on the 15-acre parcel.
Because the 50-unit limitation applies to the entire 15-acre parcel, approval of the rezoning will negatively affect the development rights of the 7.5-acre property to the north. Staff was unsuccessful in contacting the current owner of the north parcel to discuss becoming a co-applicant and addressing the residential development entitlements for the entire 15-acre parcel.
The property was created in 2020 by splitting it from the 7.5±-acre parcel to the north. It was initially classified by BCPAO as 9909 – Vacant Residential Land (Single-Family, Unplatted), which remained in place through 2025. The applicant purchased the property on January 29, 2026, and submitted an agricultural classification application (DR-482). The BCPAO staff approved the application in part and denied it in part on February 18, 2026. Only 0.15 acres was approved for bee-related use and the property use classification was changed to “6730 – Bees (Honey) Farm”. Florida law permits apiaries (bee farms) on properties not classified as agricultural if using best management requirements.
Although BCPAO currently classifies the property as a bee farm, farming and other agricultural uses are not permitted under the current R-1B zoning. The requested GU zoning would allow the proposed agricultural use, subject to applicable limitations.
On September 16, 2026, the applicant requested two exhibits identified as Concept Plan USDA Farm Layout be replaced with exhibits identified as Rebuttal submittal. The new exhibits are attached to the agenda for Council's review.
On September 22, 2026, the City Council adopted the rezoning ordinance.
On October 13, 2026, the City Council adopted a motion consistent with Section 2-26(13) of the City's Code of Ordinances to reconsider the rezoning ordinance.
Enclosed for Council's review is a Legal Addendum to the Staff Report for Ordinance No. 30-2026

The Titusville Fire Department is requesting the purchase of ten (10) new Stryker Lifepak 35 cardiac monitors and associated equipment to replace existing units that have exceeded their useful service life. The purchase will be made through the SAVVIK Cooperative Purchasing Contract No. 2024096 Medical Equipment. Stryker is the designated sole-source manufacturer and Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) provider of the LIFEPAK product line. Several of the current Lifepak 15's are no longer adequately serviceable due to outdated software and limited replacement parts, limiting the Department’s ability to maintain reliable equipment and support current emergency medical service requirements.
The total purchase cost is $607,961.26, consisting of $502,949.00 for the ten Lifepak units and $105,012.26 for the associated equipment necessary to fully outfit each unit for operational use. A trade-in credit of $3,500.00 has been applied for each of eight (8) existing Lifepak 15s, equaling $28,000.

description:
As part of the City’s ongoing efforts to improve stormwater system maintenance and drainage, staff identified the Cherrywood ditch as requiring dredging, clearing, and restoration of its downstream connection. The proposed project encompasses approximately 4,000 linear feet of ditch extending from Cherrywood Lane to SR 405.
The ditch serves residential areas and runs between homes where access for maintenance is limited. During inspections, staff determined that the existing ditch does not provide a continuous drainage connection to the culverts beneath SR 405. Near the rear property line of C&L Towing, the ditch terminates without a defined downstream outlet. Historical information indicates that the ditch previously meandered through privately owned wetlands before reaching SR 405; however, that drainage path has filled in over several decades. The City does not own or hold drainage easements over those wetlands.
Restoring a continuous, more direct drainage connection to SR 405 is an important component of this project. Clearing accumulated sediment, vegetation, and debris and reestablishing appropriate ditch grades will improve stormwater conveyance and help reduce the duration of standing water and the potential for water to back up into upstream residential areas. Addressing the downstream restriction is particularly important because maintenance of upstream portions alone would not resolve the lack of a defined outlet. Although this work will not eliminate flooding during all storm events, it is intended to improve the performance and reliability of the existing drainage system.
The high water table, wet ground conditions, and restricted access require specialized equipment, including an amphibious excavator. A walking excavator would not be suitable for completing the proposed work under these conditions. Because the City does not own this equipment and does not plan to purchase it, staff requested a proposal from SDV Services, the City’s continuing services contractor for stormwater maintenance and repairs.
Under City Contract No. CN23B019TB, SDV Services submitted a proposal totaling $699,875 to mow, grade, excavate, and remove accumulated debris and materials from the approximately 4,000-foot ditch corridor. Staff reviewed the proposal and determined that the cost is reasonable for the scope of work, specialized equipment requirements, and site constraints.
The proposed cost exceeds the funding available in the current year’s repairs and maintenance budget. The City budgeted $1,000,000 for inspection and cleaning of 20% of the stormwater system in anticipation of requirements associated with renewal of the City’s Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System (MS4) National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit. The renewed permit remains under FDEP review, and the associated permit year has not yet begun.
Given the identified drainage restriction and the importance of restoring conveyance through this residential drainage system, staff recommends approval of SDV Services proposal and reallocating $699,875 from the stormwater inspection and cleaning funding to complete this project. At the midyear budget review, staff will evaluate available fund balance and recommend additional funding to complete as much of the stormwater inspection and cleaning program as possible while addressing applicable permit requirements.
title: Ditch Clearing - Cherrywood Lane to State Road 405

Summary
On October 5, 2026, the Titusville Historic Preservation Board recommended the City Council adopt a proclamation regarding the proposed changes to the Federal Historic Preservation Regulations. The Board will also send a letter to the Federal Advisory Council on Historic Preservation (ACHP) during the public comment period.
On October 13, 2026, the City Council approved the Historic Board's request to submit a letter with concerns to the Federal Advisory Council on Historic Preservation (ACHP). The City Council also directed the staff to draft a resolution regarding opposition to the proposed changes to the Federal Historic Preservation Regulations. Enclosed for Council's review and approval is the draft resolution.
Background
The Section 106 process is a federally required review under the National Historic Preservation Act that ensures federal agencies consider the effects of their undertakings on historic properties, following four main steps: initiation, identification, assessment, and resolution. Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act provides an important opportunity for communities to share their knowledge, concerns, and ideas before federal projects or federally assisted projects move forward. Local governments and community members often have valuable knowledge about the historic places in their communities and can help identify concerns and develop solutions early in the planning process. Currently, local governments, State Historic Preservation Offices, Tribes, and Certified Local Governments are entitled to participate in Section 106 consultations.
The Federal Advisory Council on Historic Preservation (ACHP) proposed changes to the Section 106 process for historic preservation. Some of the changes include:
Ending the requirement that federal agencies seek to avoid or minimize harm to historic resources.
Only allow public participation at the discretion of federal agencies.
Eliminate the role of state and local governments in the Section 106 consultation process.
Weaken the role of tribal nations.
Eliminate protection for historic landscapes such as battlefields and national parks.
Eliminate consideration of visual and audible effects, as well as indirect effects.
The City is a consulting party in an agreement between the State, FAA and NASA to monitor the effects of the upcoming SpaceX Starship rocket. The City could be excluded from the agreement as a result of the new rule. The Federal government may also fail to notify the city of future Section 106 related impacts.
title: Resolution No. 24-2026 Historic Preservation Section 106 Process

description:
In May 2026, Brevard County E911 requested that the City officially rename the roadway and cul-de-sac located south of Golden Knights Boulevard. The request was prompted by the existence of two similarly named streets—Ponce De Leon Drive and Ponce De Leon Street—within the same mutual emergency response area, which could create confusion during emergency dispatches. The adjacent parcels are currently vacant, and the name change should not impact any property owners.
Name Significance:
Jessie Das Kirk passed away in Titusville, Florida, on March 3, 2025, and will be remembered as a beloved wife, stepmother, grandmother, and friend whose intelligence, generosity, kindness, adventurous spirit, and dedication to philanthropy touched countless lives through her family, community service, mentorship, and lifelong commitment to helping others.
Brevard County E911 approved the proposed street name, Jessie Kirk Court. The City's Public Works Department and Fire Department reviewed the proposed name change and expressed no objections.
Letters were mailed to all property owners abutting the street to provide notice of the public hearing consistent with the notification requirement in Section 30-240 of the Land Development Regulations.

On October 13, 2026, the City Council approved advertising of a public hearing for the City's intent to use the uniform methods of collecting non-ad valorem special assessment for the cost of providing fire protection services against benefited real property located within the incorporated area of the City of Titusville as authorized under Section 197.3632, Florida Statues
The public hearing for this item includes the adoption of Resolution 27-2026, which, if adopted, will be mailed to the Florida Department of Revenue, the Brevard County Tax Collector and the Brevard County Property Appraiser as notice of the City's planned use of a non-ad valorem special assessment for a percentage of the cost of providing fire protection services beginning with the FY28 fiscal year which begins Ocotber 1, 2027.
If adopted, the City will bring a consultant back to City Council on December 8, 2026, for approval of the study.
It is recommended that City Council hold a public hearing for this item and adopt Resolution 27-2026 stating the City's intent to use the uniform methods of collecting non-ad valorem special assessment for the cost of providing fire protection services against benefited real property located within the incorporated area of the City of Titusville.

description: Section 163.3177(3)(b), Florida Statutes, requires the City to annually update the Five-Year Capital Improvement Program (CIP) contained within the Capital Improvements Element (CIE) of the Comprehensive Plan. State law requires all local governments to include a CIE in their Comprehensive Plans to address the need for and location of public facilities. The CIE must establish principles for the construction, extension, or expansion of public facility capacity, as well as strategies for correcting existing public facility deficiencies necessary to implement the Comprehensive Plan. The planning horizon for the CIE is five (5) years.
title: Ordinance No. 46-2026 - Capital Improvements Element of the Comprehensive Plan Annual Update of the 5-Year Schedule of Capital Improvements (FY 2027–2031)

description: The applicant, Mr. Robert Telfer, Jr., on behalf of Highway 50 Beneficiaries, LLC, is requesting approval of a Small-Scale Comprehensive Plan Amendment (SSA) with rezoning to establish consistent commercial future land use and zoning across the subject property. Approval of the request would eliminate the existing fragmented land use and zoning by providing a unified commercial development pattern to enhance the overall marketability and development potential of the property. The current Low Density Residential and High Density Residential future land use designations, as well as the Single-Family Medium Density (R-1B) and Multifamily High Density Residential (R-3) zoning districts, do not permit commercial uses. The property is located on Cheney Highway, between Worth Avenue and Zoltan Drive, generally south-west of the Publix Super Market shopping center at 2000 Cheney Highway. The subject property includes four parcels/lots and has three different zoning districts and land use designations.
title: Small Scale Amendment Application No. 4-2026 - 2305 Cheney Highway

description:
The staff recommended the City Council amend the minimum parking requirements for mini-warehouse. Section 28-214(d)(1)g requires one (1) parking space for each of the twenty-five (25) storage cubicles and two (2) spaces for the manager's quarters. The staff believed this requirement is excessive and may contribute to detrimental effects on the natural environment and impose disproportionate burdens on property owners. The City's parking standards for warehouse would have applied if the ordinance was adopted. The staff drafted an ordinance based on City Council's May 26, 2020, directive to review the Land Development Regulations to encourage redevelopment.
On September 8, 2026, the Council inquired about adding an open space requirement for mini-warehouse developments. The staff recommended one of two options. "The parking requirements may be reduced with an equivalent area of bioswale and/or rain garden."
"Shall provide an additional twenty (20) percent vegetation and open space not to include required buffers."
On September 22, 2026, Council directed the staff to draft a new ordinance utilizing both conditions and allow parking requirements to be reduced if open space and low impact development (LID) best management practices (BMP) were provided. The Counciul further requested the draft ordinance be presented for review prior to publication and the scheduling of public hearings. Enclosed for Council's review is the ordinance.

description:
As a summary and reminder, on May 30, 2026, at the City Council Strategic Planning Retreat, Council requested the City Attorney's Office research and provide information regarding Procedures for Amending Sovereignty Submerged Lands Leases; Expanding Uses at Titusville Municipal Marina, and Surrounding Parks. On June 30, 2026, the City Attorney's Office provided Council an initial memorandum in response to that request.
On July 14, 2026, the City Council reviewed the City Attorney's Office legal memorandum that was provided to the City Council on June 30, 2026. At that time, the City Council requested a special meeting to review the expansion of uses at Marina Park and the City Marina.
An additional memorandum was emailed to the Mayor and Council, City Manager, Assistant City Manager, and to the City Clerk on August 31, 2026.
It is recommended that City Council provide direction on expanded uses of Marina Park and the City Marina.
